terms.title: Son of Man
terms.gist: In the Gospels this is the title Jesus most often uses of himself. In the Old Testament the phrase can simply mean 'a human being' (God addresses Ezekiel this way again and again), but in Daniel 7 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting rule from the Ancient of Days. Jesus draws on both: he is truly one of us, and he is the figure who judges and reigns.

terms.title: Son of God
terms.gist: In the Old Testament 'son of God' can name Israel as a people (Exodus 4:22), the Davidic king (Psalm 2:7), or the angels. In the Gospels it moves from a royal and messianic title to a confession of who Jesus is: at the baptism and the Transfiguration the Father's voice calls him his beloved Son, and the centurion at the cross confesses him.

terms.title: Son of David
terms.gist: God promised David a son whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7). The Gospels open by naming Jesus 'son of David' and the title is used by the blind and by the crowds who ask for mercy, and who greet him at Jerusalem. It is a royal and messianic title that Jesus accepts, and then stretches: how can David call his own descendant 'Lord'?

terms.title: Kingdom of God / of heaven
terms.gist: The heart of Jesus' preaching. It is not a place but God's kingly rule breaking into history: already begun in Jesus' words and works, still to come in glory. Matthew mostly says 'kingdom of heaven', a reverent way of avoiding the name of God; Mark, Luke and Paul say 'kingdom of God'. Most parables begin 'the kingdom is like...'.

terms.title: Lamb of God
terms.gist: John the Baptist points to Jesus and says 'Behold the Lamb of God, who takest away the sin of the world.' Several Old Testament lambs lie behind it: the Passover lamb whose blood saved Israel, the daily offering in the Temple, Isaac's ram, and the silent lamb of Isaiah 53. At Mass the people hear these words before Communion.

terms.title: 'I AM'
terms.gist: At the burning bush God gives Moses his name, 'I AM WHO AM' (Exodus 3:14). In John's Gospel Jesus says 'I am' with a predicate (the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection, the way, the true vine) and also, strikingly, on its own. His hearers pick up stones: they heard him taking the divine name.

terms.title: 'Amen, amen, I say to you'
terms.gist: 'Amen' means 'so be it' or 'truly', and in Jewish speech it comes at the end of what someone else has said. Jesus does something unheard of: he begins his own sayings with it. John doubles it. It marks the words as weighty and spoken on his own authority.

terms.title: Emmanuel
terms.gist: 'God with us.' The name comes from the sign Isaiah gave to King Ahaz (Isaiah 7:14) and is applied by Matthew to the child conceived of the Virgin Mary. The Gospel of Matthew begins with this name and ends with Jesus' promise 'I am with you all days'.

terms.title: The Word (Logos)
terms.gist: John begins by saying that the Word was in the beginning with God, was God, and became flesh. In the Old Testament God's word creates ('God said... and it was so'), speaks through the prophets and is spoken of almost like a person; in Wisdom literature Wisdom is with God at creation. John says all of this has a face: Jesus.

terms.title: New covenant
terms.gist: Jeremiah promised a new covenant written on hearts, not on stone (Jeremiah 31). At the Last Supper Jesus calls the cup 'the new covenant in my blood', and Hebrews says he is its mediator. In older English Bibles the same Greek word is translated 'testament', which is why the two halves of the Bible are called Old and New Testament.

terms.title: Day of the Lord
terms.gist: A day when God acts decisively: sometimes judgement on Israel and the nations, sometimes rescue. The prophets use it as a warning (Amos says it is darkness, not light); the New Testament speaks of it as the day of Christ's return, coming 'like a thief'.

terms.title: The remnant
terms.gist: Through judgement a few survive, and God builds on them. Isaiah named a son 'a remnant shall return'. Paul says that in his own day too there is 'a remnant according to the election of grace', that is, Jewish believers in Christ.

terms.title: Passover (Pasch)
terms.gist: The night God freed Israel from Egypt, remembered every year with a lamb, unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Jesus' death falls at the Passover, and the Church calls Easter the Pasch. Paul says 'Christ our Pasch is sacrificed', and each Mass remembers the new Passover.

terms.title: Manna
terms.gist: The bread that fell each morning in the wilderness, enough for the day and no more. In John 6 the crowd cites it as the sign they want; Jesus answers that the true bread from heaven is the one the Father is now giving, and speaks of eating his flesh. The Church sees in the manna a type of the Eucharist.

terms.title: Abba
terms.gist: An Aramaic word for father used by children at home, kept untranslated in Greek texts. Jesus prays 'Abba' in Gethsemane, and Paul says the Spirit makes us cry 'Abba, Father'. It shows how intimately Jesus spoke to God, and invites us to the same.

terms.title: Hosanna
terms.gist: From the Hebrew cry 'save us, we pray' (Psalm 118:25). By Jesus' day it had become a shout of praise at festivals. The crowds use it when he enters Jerusalem, and the Church takes it into the Sanctus at Mass.

terms.title: Alleluia (Hallelujah)
terms.gist: 'Praise the Lord.' It stands at the head or end of many psalms and, in the New Testament, only in Revelation 19, where the whole company of heaven sings it. The Church sings it before the Gospel and keeps it silent in Lent.

terms.title: Selah
terms.gist: A word in the Psalms whose exact meaning is lost. It is thought to mark a pause, an instrument interlude or a lifting of the voice. It appears 71 times in the Hebrew Psalter. The Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims leave it out, which is why you will find it in some translations and not in others.

terms.title: The good shepherd
terms.gist: In the Old Testament God is Israel's shepherd and kings and leaders are called shepherds, often failing. Ezekiel promises that God himself will shepherd his scattered sheep and set up one shepherd, David. Jesus says 'I am the good shepherd' and lays down his life for the sheep; the early Church loved the image.

terms.title: Bread of life
terms.gist: The title Jesus takes after feeding the five thousand. Moses fed Israel with manna; Jesus offers himself as bread that gives eternal life. The later part of John 6, about eating his flesh and drinking his blood, has been read in the Church from the earliest centuries as speaking of the Eucharist.

terms.title: Light of the world
terms.gist: Said by Jesus at the Feast of Tabernacles, when great lamps burned in the Temple court, and again when he heals the man born blind. In Matthew 5:14 he says the same of his disciples. Light is also the first thing God made (Genesis 1:3) and the image of his law and salvation in the prophets.

terms.title: Fear of the Lord
terms.gist: In Scripture this is not terror but reverent awe before God, which leads to love and obedience. Proverbs calls it the beginning of wisdom, and Isaiah lists it among the gifts of the Spirit. The Church names it one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

terms.title: The Holy of Holies
terms.gist: The innermost room of the Tabernacle and the Temple, where the ark stood, entered only by the high priest once a year on the Day of Atonement. When Jesus died the Temple veil in front of it was torn in two, and Hebrews says that Christ has entered the true holy place in heaven.

terms.title: The Ark of the Covenant
terms.gist: The gilded chest that held the tablets of the law, with the mercy seat on top, where God's presence met his people. It led them through the Jordan, fell into Philistine hands, and was brought to Jerusalem by David. The Fathers saw in it a sign of Mary, who carried the Word; Revelation shows the ark in heaven's temple.

terms.title: Justified by faith
terms.gist: Paul's central teaching: no one is made right with God by the works of the law but by God's gift, received in faith. Abraham 'believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice' (Genesis 15:6), and Paul says that is the pattern. The Catholic Church teaches that this faith is alive in love and brings real renewal, not only a change of status (Council of Trent).

terms.title: 'I will build my church'
terms.gist: Jesus' words to Simon after his confession: 'Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.' Peter's name means 'rock'; the Church has read in these words Christ's gift of a leading place to Peter and his successors, and the passage is one of the most discussed in Scripture. Only here and in Matthew 18:17 does Jesus use the word 'church'.

terms.title: Ancient of days
terms.gist: In Daniel's vision, thrones are set up and an Ancient of days takes his seat, his clothing white as snow. Then one like a son of man is brought before him and given dominion. The phrase names God, as old as time and its judge.

terms.title: 'My beloved Son'
terms.gist: The Father's voice at Jesus' baptism and again at the Transfiguration. The words join Psalm 2:7 ('Thou art my son'), Genesis 22 ('thy beloved son') and Isaiah 42:1 (the chosen servant): kingship, sacrifice and service in a single sentence.

terms.title: The sign of Jonah
terms.gist: When asked for a sign Jesus says none will be given except 'the sign of Jonas the prophet'. Matthew explains it as three days in the heart of the earth; Luke ties it to Jonah's preaching. Both point to the Resurrection.

terms.title: The bridegroom
terms.gist: The prophets picture God as husband of his people (Hosea, Isaiah, Ezekiel), and the Song of Songs was read in that light. Jesus calls himself the bridegroom when he is asked why his disciples do not fast, and tells parables of the wedding feast. Revelation ends with the marriage of the Lamb.

terms.title: Mammon
terms.gist: A word from the Aramaic for wealth or property. Jesus personifies it as a rival master: 'You cannot serve God and mammon.' The word was kept untranslated in Greek and Latin.

terms.title: Maranatha
terms.gist: An Aramaic prayer that Paul leaves untranslated at the end of 1 Corinthians. It can be divided two ways, 'Our Lord, come!' (marana tha) or 'Our Lord has come' (maran atha). The Church has long prayed it with the first meaning, and the Book of Revelation ends with the same cry in Greek.
